name: Prize crossword No 23,113
preamble: This crossword is sponsored by Bells. The sponsor's products will appear in the diagonals, three in one and one (as it might be indexed) in the other. The third is represented at 26.

clue.text: Squat writer at opening of Jersey enclosure

indicators.note: an opening is where something starts, so only the first letter is kept

blocks.note: first letter of Jersey
a pen is an enclosure for animals

explanation.surface: A stocky author sits by the gate of a field on Jersey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' looks like the second half of the definition only, but 'Squat writer' as a whole is the answer; the pen of the wordplay is the farmyard kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A J-pen is an old broad-nibbed steel pen, its stubby point making it a short, thick writing tool.

clue.text: Somerset House supplies colour in Kingston town

blocks.note: a tint is a shade of colour
taken as written
Kingston upon Hull is the full name of the Yorkshire port

explanation.surface: The London building that kept birth records sends paint to a riverside town.
explanation.walkthrough: Somerset House is a famous London building, but here it is a house in the county of Somerset: Tintinhull House, a National Trust garden. Hull is officially Kingston upon Hull.
explanation.definitionFit: Tintinhull is a village in Somerset whose manor house and garden are owned by the National Trust.

clue.text: An ode I translated in complete ignorance

indicators.note: a translated text is rendered into another form, so these letters take a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone renders a poem into another language without understanding a word of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads naturally as a translator's confession; 'translated' does the rearranging of the first three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Having no idea is the everyday idiom for knowing nothing whatever about a matter.

clue.text: Annoyed with laureate Robert? Wait till you reach them!

definitions.note: the proverb 'don't cross your bridges until you come to them'

blocks.note: cross means annoyed
Robert Bridges was Poet Laureate from 1913 to 1930

explanation.surface: Someone irritated by a poet is told to be patient until they meet him.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the proverb 'don't cross your bridges before you come to them'; the advice to wait points at the action itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb warns against tackling problems early, so the act to delay until arrival is crossing those bridges.

clue.text: Game that sounds obscene in company

indicators.note: something that sounds a certain way is judged by the ear, not the spelling
being in something means sitting within its walls

blocks.note: CO is the standard abbreviation for company
lewd means obscene; LUED is said the same way

explanation.surface: A party game that turns out to be rude when played with others.
explanation.walkthrough: The sound of an obscene word is spelt unconventionally so it can sit between the two letters of the company abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Cluedo is the British name for the murder-mystery board game called Clue in North America.

clue.text: Is it possible for Edward to succeed to the throne? It will need a widget

blocks.note: can asks whether something is possible
Ned is a pet form of Edward
to succeed is to BE ER, the reigning monarch (Elizabeth Regina)

explanation.surface: A constitutional question about Prince Edward becoming king, oddly needing a gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: ER is the Queen's cipher, Elizabeth Regina, so 'to be ER' is to occupy the throne. A widget is the gas-filled ball in a can of stout that makes it foam like draught.
explanation.definitionFit: Brewers put a small nitrogen capsule called a widget into tins of beer to give a creamy head when opened.

clue.text: Help yourselves to old medal before crazy guy sets out

indicators.note: something crazy is disordered, so the letters lose their order
set out means laid out afresh, a second hint at rearranging

blocks.note: the British Empire Medal, discontinued in the UK in 1993
taken as written

explanation.surface: A host tells guests to grab an old medal before a madman heads off.
explanation.walkthrough: BEM, the British Empire Medal, was stopped for UK recipients in the 1990s, hence 'old'. 'Before' places it ahead of the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Be my guests is a hospitable invitation telling several people to take whatever they want freely.

clue.text: Solar put right outside 51 across

indicators.note: to be outside something is to surround it on either side

blocks.note: to heal is to make well again
LI is 51 in Roman numerals
AC is the crossword abbreviation for across

explanation.surface: Like a grid cross-reference: fix something outside the clue numbered 51 across.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no 51 across in the grid: the cross-reference is a disguise for a Roman numeral and an abbreviation, which together sit inside the healing word.
explanation.definitionFit: Heliacal means relating to the sun, especially of a star rising just before sunrise.

clue.text: Casts without a note produce groovy sounds

definitions.note: both senses at once: grooves and flute music

indicators.note: the old sense of without is outside, so one word wraps the other

blocks.note: to cast is to fling
ut is the old name for the first note of the scale, now doh

explanation.surface: Members of a cast without one musical note make cool, trendy music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' reads as lacking, but here it means outside. Ut is the medieval name for the note now called doh.
explanation.definitionFit: Flutings are both the grooves cut into a column and the warbling notes of a flute, so groovy sounds fits doubly.

clue.text: Daddy, I'm a lion asking for a boat

blocks.note: pa is an informal word for father
what a lion would say of itself: I roar

explanation.surface: A child pretending to be a lion begs their father for a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: The child's words, 'Pa, I roar', run together into the name of the craft they want.
explanation.definitionFit: A pair-oar is a rowing boat for two rowers, each pulling a single oar.

clue.text: Would you like an answer, if you grasp fields of telepathy?

definitions.note: the answer is the reply to the question that precedes it

indicators.note: to grasp is to hold in the hand, so one piece is held by another

blocks.note: the question being answered; it frames the definition and gives no letters
ye is the old plural you
ESP, extrasensory perception, covers telepathy
a lea is a meadow or field

explanation.surface: An offer to answer, conditional on the listener understanding mind-reading.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a question, and the answer is its eager reply. Within the wordplay, 'fields of telepathy' is read as the field-word following the telepathy abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: When someone asks 'Would you like...?', the polite affirmative reply accepting the offer is this phrase.

clue.text: On introduction I may turn to the Treasury, No 5

definitions.text: On introduction I may turn to the Treasury, No 5

blocks.clueFragment: On introduction I may turn to
blocks.note: surface: a newcomer says what they will become when presented; setter: the old courtly phrase a person used of themself on being introduced, standing for 'I'
surface: a government department and an address; setter: someone employed there is a civil servant

explanation.walkthrough: A formal speaker once bowed and called themself 'your servant' instead of saying I; a Treasury official is a servant of the state. The 'No 5' tag is left unexplained here.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase was a courteous self-description used when meeting someone, and civil servants work at the Treasury.

clue.text: Like this house off the Charing Cross Road?

definitions.note: a location phrase standing for the district

blocks.note: so means in this way
HO is the abbreviation for house

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a particular building stands just off a busy London street.
explanation.walkthrough: Charing Cross Road is a London street of bookshops; the district named lies just west of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Soho is the central London entertainment district bounded on its eastern side by that very road.

clue.text: Say you start on the answer, will this keep you clean?

indicators.note: to say a word is to speak it, so the sound matters rather than spelling
a start is only the beginning, so the rest of the word is dropped

blocks.note: the letters EU are pronounced like the word you
the opening of SOLUTION, which is what an answer is

explanation.surface: Asking whether getting going on the reply will keep someone tidy.
explanation.walkthrough: EUSOL is a chlorine antiseptic whose name stands for Edinburgh University Solution Of Lime, so the 'solution' in the wordplay is apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Eusol is an antiseptic wash once used to clean wounds and keep infection away.

clue.text: Male in place of mail, formerly the way for a stopover

definitions.text: formerly the way for a stopover

blocks.note: surface: a man swapped for letters; setter: STAG (a male deer) put in place of the mail (post) of a coaching stop

blocks.clueFragment: formerly the way for a stopover
blocks.note: the old coaching system changed horses at fixed stops along the road

explanation.walkthrough: Mail coaches ran in stages, stopping at inns to change horses; the playful first half turns the place name into a stag sitting at a post.
explanation.definitionFit: A staging post was a regular halt on a coach route where travellers rested and horses were changed.

clue.text: Musically famous

blocks.note: first meaning: written in musical notes
second meaning: well known, celebrated

explanation.walkthrough: The two words read like one phrase about a celebrated musician; they are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A tune can be noted, set down in notation, and a person can be noted, widely renowned.

clue.text: Laureate Robert holding church service in the Cotswolds

definitions.note: a location phrase standing for the village

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it within, so one piece surrounds the rest

blocks.note: Robert Southey was Poet Laureate from 1813 to 1843
CE is the Church of England
the Royal Navy is the senior service

explanation.surface: A poet laureate holds a church service in a Cotswold village.
explanation.walkthrough: After Bridges at 4, a second Laureate Robert appears: Southey. The service is the armed forces kind, not a church one.
explanation.definitionFit: South Cerney is a village near Cirencester in the Cotswold hills of Gloucestershire.

clue.text: Misplaced paintwork

indicators.note: to work material is to knead and reshape it, so the letters are reshaped

blocks.note: the first five letters of the printed word, the rest being the signal to rearrange

explanation.surface: Decoration slapped on in the wrong place.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder and the indicator are fused into one printed word, paintwork.
explanation.definitionFit: Inapt means unsuitable or out of place, as a misplaced remark would be.

clue.text: Suit one when it's gone home by commercial backing inside

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the order of letters runs the other way
inside means within something else, so this piece goes into another

blocks.note: the SU, Soviet Union, was a union, a single entity, before it ceased to exist
a nest is a bird's home
taken as written
an ad is a commercial

explanation.surface: Clothes worn once a person has left for home, paid for by an advertiser.
explanation.walkthrough: The Soviet Union, SU, is the union that is gone. Read the reversed pair inside the home word.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunday best is the smart suit of clothes kept for church and special occasions.

clue.text: Desirable semi, catch for the methodical

indicators.note: estate agents call a property desirable once it has been done up, and these letters are done up anew

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An estate agent's attractive semi-detached house, a real catch for an orderly buyer.
explanation.walkthrough: A semi is a semi-detached house, the British suburban home sharing one wall with its neighbour. The clue's indicator is unusual; it is the only word left to signal the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Schematic describes something set out according to a scheme or system, hence orderly and methodical.

clue.text: T? Insert extra one into small jumper for new opening

indicators.note: to insert is to put something inside something else
an opening is a beginning, so only a first letter is kept

blocks.note: an adjunct is an extra, supplementary thing
I is the Roman numeral one
roo is short for kangaroo, a jumper
first letter of new

explanation.surface: A tailor's instruction for adding a panel into a child's sweater to make a new neck opening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' is a sweater in Britain, but here it is the kangaroo, shortened. The extra and the numeral go between the two letter-pairs of the kangaroo-plus-initial.
explanation.definitionFit: A T-junction is a road junction shaped like the letter, so a lone T with a question mark defines one by example.

clue.text: Yesterday's French containing anything less modest?

indicators.note: to contain is to hold within, so one word surrounds another

blocks.note: hier is French for yesterday
aught is an old word for anything

explanation.surface: Asking whether old French styles were any less humble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yesterday's French' means the French for yesterday, not old French.
explanation.definitionFit: Haughtier means prouder and more arrogant, the opposite of being modest.

clue.text: Robber girl, the first to be put inside

indicators.note: putting something inside means placing it within another word

blocks.note: Hester is a girl's name
I is the Roman numeral one, the first

explanation.surface: A female thief is the first of her gang to be jailed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put inside' suggests prison, but it is the instruction to place the numeral within the name.
explanation.definitionFit: A heister is a robber, from heist, the American slang for a hold-up or robbery.

clue.text: Prescribed list for The Times?

definitions.note: an adjective standing for the things a doctor prescribes

blocks.note: a table is a list of figures
T is the symbol for time, so times are T's

explanation.surface: A set reading list for the staff of a London newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Times is a British newspaper, but here it is just the plural of the time symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Tablets are pills, the commonest form of medicine a doctor prescribes for a patient.

clue.text: A pretty good pupil to the Queen in Iolanthe

definitions.note: a location phrase standing for a character in the opera

blocks.note: tol-lol is old slang for pretty good, passable
L is a learner
ER, Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: A fairly able student plays opposite the Fairy Queen in a Gilbert and Sullivan opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Iolanthe has a Fairy Queen, so 'the Queen' fits the surface, but it is the royal cipher. Gilbert named the earl after the slang word.
explanation.definitionFit: Earl Tolloller is one of the two foppish peers who court Phyllis in Gilbert and Sullivan's Iolanthe.

clue.text: Black Labour leader broken by a vote for the Iron Lady

indicators.note: something broken by an intruder is split apart with that intruder in the gap

blocks.note: B is black, as on pencils
Clement Attlee led the Labour Party and was Prime Minister 1945 to 1951
taken as written
a voter marks a cross on the ballot

explanation.surface: A gloomy day for a Labour leader: a vote goes to Margaret Thatcher.
explanation.walkthrough: The Iron Lady is Margaret Thatcher's nickname; she was famously formidable, and the answer is a jokey word for such a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A battle-axe is a domineering, aggressive older woman, and Thatcher was often characterised that way.

clue.text: American city to hawk African one?

blocks.note: Los Angeles
gos is an old short form of goshawk

explanation.surface: A US city peddling its wares to an African one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hawk' looks like a verb meaning to sell, but it is the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Lagos is the largest city of Nigeria, so it is another city, this time in Africa.

clue.text: Sovereign part of 10 in riverside structure: dairymaid can take it

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for the vessel

indicators.note: being in something means lying within its walls

blocks.note: a watermill stands by a river
a king is a sovereign
the first three letters of the answer at 10, PAIR-OAR

explanation.surface: A monarch's barge moored at a riverside mill, cheerfully used by a milkmaid.
explanation.walkthrough: Ten is the clue number of the boat answer; take part of it. 'Can' hints at a container for milk.
explanation.definitionFit: A milking pail is the bucket a dairymaid holds under the cow, so she takes it to the shed.

clue.text: Bird out of temper with Cathy's grange

blocks.note: a thrush is a songbird
cross means bad-tempered

explanation.surface: An irritable bird lives at a country house.
explanation.walkthrough: Thrushcross Grange is the Lintons' house in Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights, where Cathy goes to live; the preamble's 'third' Bell novel is represented here.
explanation.definitionFit: In Wuthering Heights, Catherine Earnshaw marries Edgar Linton and becomes mistress of Thrushcross Grange.

clue.text: Fool wants cleaner situation

blocks.note: a char is a cleaning lady
the lie of the land is how things stand

explanation.surface: An idiot is looking for a job as a cleaner.
explanation.walkthrough: A char, or charwoman, is an old British term for a cleaner.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a charlie is a silly person, as in 'a right charlie'.

clue.text: Bearings subtending a right angle have the smell of ageing

blocks.note: south-east and north-east are compass bearings ninety degrees apart
a scent is a smell

explanation.surface: Old machine bearings at right angles give off the odour of age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bearings' suggests machine parts; they are compass directions, two of them a quarter-turn apart.
explanation.definitionFit: Senescent means growing old, from the Latin senescere, to grow old.

clue.text: Historian not speaking American?

blocks.note: tacit means unspoken
US, the United States

explanation.surface: A chronicler who refuses to speak the American language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not speaking American' sounds like a language barrier; it is a word for silent next to a country abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacitus was a Roman historian whose Annals and Histories chronicle the early emperors.

clue.text: Play scene gives Lancelot Christian conversion

indicators.note: a conversion changes something into a new form

blocks.note: taken as written
Chr. is an abbreviation for Christian

explanation.surface: A dramatic scene in which the Arthurian knight becomes a Christian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play scene' looks theatrical, but the play is musical: a place where musicians play.
explanation.definitionFit: A concert hall is the venue where orchestras play, so it is the scene of playing.

clue.text: Soldiers carrying pounds of baggage

indicators.note: to carry is to hold within, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a troop is a body of soldiers
L is a pound, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: An army unit lugs heavy kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Baggage' looks like luggage, but it is an old, insulting word for a woman of loose morals.
explanation.definitionFit: Baggage was an old term for a disreputable woman, just as trollop is.

clue.text: Earnest author admitting my appropriate retraction

indicators.note: to retract is to draw back, so the letters run backwards
to admit is to let in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a parent is the author of a child
taken as written
apt means appropriate

explanation.surface: A serious writer owns up to taking back a fitting remark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Earnest' looks like an adjective for the author; it is the noun, as in earnest money paid to bind a deal.
explanation.definitionFit: An earnest is a token sum paid in advance to seal a bargain, a portion of the full price.

clue.text: Greek is tough!

blocks.note: first meaning: a citizen of ancient Sparta
second meaning: austere, hardy

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a complaint about learning the language; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Spartans were famed for their harsh discipline, which gave the adjective for austere toughness.

clue.text: Sale of hot article in place of electrical conversion

indicators.note: being in something means lying within its walls

blocks.note: a substation steps electrical voltage up or down
H is hot, as on taps
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Stolen goods are being sold off at the local electricity substation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot article' suggests stolen goods, but it is two separate abbreviations slipped into the power installation.
explanation.definitionFit: Subhastation is a rare word for a public auction, from the Latin sub hasta, under the spear where auctions were held.

clue.text: Report of watchman getting affectionate greeting, trying to go in?

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: a sentry is a watchman
petal is a fond form of address, as in 'hello, petal'

explanation.surface: A guard on duty is greeted warmly as he tries to get indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: Petal is a northern English endearment like love or dear. The definition is playful: a force pulling towards the centre is trying to get in.
explanation.definitionFit: Centripetal means tending towards the centre, so a centripetal force is always trying to move inwards.

clue.text: Italian girl drinking a bottle in Giglio's kingdom

indicators.note: drinking takes something inside, so one piece swallows another

blocks.note: Pia is an Italian girl's name
taken as written
a flagon is a large bottle

explanation.surface: A young Italian woman sips wine in an Italian prince's realm.
explanation.walkthrough: Giglio is the prince who becomes king in Thackeray's comic fairy tale The Rose and the Ring.
explanation.definitionFit: Paflagonia is the imaginary kingdom in Thackeray's The Rose and the Ring, of which Giglio is the rightful heir.

clue.text: Ordinal for solvers with some theology?

blocks.note: a jokey plural of thou, the old form of you, addressing everyone solving
and means with
Th is the abbreviation for theology, as in the degree ThD

explanation.surface: A religious puzzle setter ranks the people tackling his crossword.
explanation.walkthrough: An ordinal number gives a position in order, like first or tenth. The solvers are addressed in the old second person.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordinal numbers mark position in a sequence, and thousandth is the one for position 1,000.

clue.text: Tetchy characters from Austria boil

indicators.note: characters are letters, and taking letters from words frees them to be set in any order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Grumpy Austrians lose their tempers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boil' looks like the verb of the surface, but its letters join the country's in the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Atrabilious means melancholy or irritable, from black bile, the humour once blamed for bad temper.

clue.text: First, the first drink to go in by the mouth

indicators.note: going in means entering another word

blocks.note: orally means by mouth
I is the Roman numeral one, the first
gin is a drink

explanation.surface: Instructions for a medicine: first the opening dose, swallowed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' and 'the first' sit side by side; the first is the definition and the second the numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Originally means in the first place or at first, before later changes.

clue.text: Light associate obtained from Samson's lion

blocks.note: first meaning: the word paired with light in a familiar phrase for gentle good humour
second meaning: what Samson's riddle says came out of the strong, the honey in a lion's carcass

explanation.walkthrough: In Judges 14, Samson finds bees and honey in the body of a lion he killed; his riddle says sweetness came out of the strong.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'sweetness and light' pairs the two words, and the honey from the lion was the sweetness of the riddle.

clue.text: S-scratcher holds out with demand for good turns

indicators.note: to hold is to keep within, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: taken as written
a claw scratches
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone scratching an S holds out, demanding kind deeds.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen splits off a lone letter. Scouts promise to do a good turn every day.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scout Law sets out the rules Scouts follow, famously including doing a good turn daily.

clue.text: Welshman said thanks for silks

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the sound is what counts

blocks.note: Taffy is a nickname for a Welshman and ta is thanks

explanation.surface: A Welshman says thank you for some silk fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: Taffy, from the Welsh Dafydd, is an old British nickname for a Welshman; ta is British slang for thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: Taffeta is a crisp, lustrous fabric traditionally woven from silk, so taffetas are silks.

clue.text: City female's diminutive female with lots of transport

indicators.note: lots of something is most of it but not all, so a letter goes

blocks.note: F is female
lorries, the British word for trucks, without the final S

explanation.surface: A tiny woman from the city surrounded by heavy traffic.
explanation.walkthrough: The city is Florence, also a woman's name; the answer is its pet form. 'Diminutive female' tempts as the definition, but female is the wordplay letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Florrie is a familiar short form of the name Florence, which is also an Italian city.

clue.text: It's piping with half a pipe for almost vinegary setter

indicators.note: half of a word keeps one side and loses the other
almost means not quite, so the word stops short of its end

blocks.note: the second half of pipe
acetic means vinegary; its last letter is dropped
the setter refers to himself

explanation.surface: A plumber's instruction about joining a sour-tempered crossword setter's pipes.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition recalls Richard III's 'this weak piping time of peace': piping refers to the shepherd's pipe played in quiet times.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's 'piping time of peace' made piping an epithet for peaceful days, when pipes replace drums.

clue.text: Dark Blues to be afraid the gun will not be audible

blocks.note: Oxford University, whose sports colour is dark blue
taken as written
to fear is to be afraid
a gun, in the sense of a marksman, is a shot

explanation.surface: Oxford's rowers dread the starting gun being too far off to hear.
explanation.walkthrough: In British university sport Oxford are the Dark Blues and Cambridge the Light Blues, as in the Boat Race.
explanation.definitionFit: Out of earshot means beyond the range of hearing, so a sound there cannot be heard.

clue.text: The golden spirit has missed Tom, unfortunate child

indicators.note: to miss something is to go without it, so letters are left out

blocks.note: or is gold in heraldry
a phantom is a ghost
the name, removed from the end of the ghost word

explanation.surface: A golden ghost that has failed to find Tom, a pitiable child.
explanation.walkthrough: Or is heraldry's term for gold, common in crosswords. Tom is not a person to find but the tail of the ghost word.
explanation.definitionFit: An orphan is a child whose parents have died, the classic unfortunate child of fiction.

clue.text: Chemist such as Gauguin sets New York this test

indicators.note: a test puts material through trials that can rearrange it

blocks.note: taken as written
NY is New York
taken as written

explanation.surface: A chemist who paints like Gauguin sets an exam for New York.
explanation.walkthrough: Gauguin led the Synthetist painters of Pont-Aven, so he fits as a second definition alongside the chemist who synthesises compounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A synthesist builds compounds by synthesis, and Gauguin's Synthetism movement made him a synthesist in painting.

clue.text: Number of importance first off

indicators.note: with its first taken off, a word loses its opening letter

blocks.note: weighty means important

explanation.surface: A figure that matters most, then gets dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' could be a song or anaesthetic; here it is a plain number.
explanation.definitionFit: Eighty is the cardinal number eight times ten, so it is simply a number.

clue.text: See 39 across
Dealing in the wind

definitions.note: a location phrase for the word that precedes wind

blocks.note: first meaning: buying and selling, commerce
second meaning: the word found in the name of the steady tropical wind

explanation.walkthrough: 'In the wind' suggests a rumour; it means the word sits in a wind's name, the trade wind.
explanation.definitionFit: Trade means commerce, and the trade winds are the steady easterlies that carried merchant ships.

clue.text: Inescapable order to go quickly dispatched again

blocks.note: the Order of Merit
to nip is to go somewhere quickly
re-sent means sent again

explanation.surface: An urgent instruction to hurry is posted once more, impossible to avoid.
explanation.walkthrough: The OM, Order of Merit, is a British honour; 'resent' here is re-sent, not the verb of grudging.
explanation.definitionFit: Something omnipresent is everywhere at once, so there is no escaping it.

clue.text: Very good money

blocks.note: first meaning: splendid, excellent
second meaning: slang for a thousand pounds or dollars

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as praise for a good salary; the phrase and the noun are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means splendid or fine, and is also slang for a sum of a thousand pounds or dollars.

clue.text: Fresh as the morning librarian's report?

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: Melvil Dewey devised the library classification system

explanation.surface: A cheerful librarian files a report bright and early.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dewey Decimal system classifies library books by number, so the librarian's name is Dewey.
explanation.definitionFit: Dewy means wet with dew, and so fresh like the early morning grass.

clue.text: A means of saving conceals the end of Michael Craig

definitions.note: the second word of a two-word name

indicators.note: to conceal is to hide inside, so one piece is held within another

blocks.note: taken as written
